summary: This Docker Compose configuration defines a service called 'markitdown' that builds a container from a local Dockerfile, mounts the current directory as a workspace, and runs with restricted security settings like dropped capabilities and read-only filesystem to minimize attack surface.

explanations.8: This passes the UID (user ID) from your host machine into the Docker build, defaulting to 1000 if not set—this makes files created inside the container owned by your user instead of root.
explanations.9: Same idea as UID but for GID (group ID), ensuring the container group matches your host machine's group.
explanations.11: This mounts your current directory (the dot) into the container at /workspace; 'cached' is a performance hint for Docker Desktop on Mac.
explanations.12: The tmpfs sections create temporary in-memory filesystems that disappear when the container stops, useful for temporary files.
explanations.13: This limits the /tmp mount to 64 megabytes and prevents executing files or using setuid binaries from it—security hardening.
explanations.15: Dropping ALL capabilities removes all special Linux permissions from the container, so it can't do dangerous things like change network settings.
explanations.18: This prevents the container from gaining new privileges even if a process inside tries to escalate—another security lock.
explanations.19: The filesystem is read-only by default, so the container can't modify files unless explicitly allowed (like /tmp and /run).
explanations.20: This makes the container run as your user and group instead of root, reducing the damage if something inside gets compromised.
